summary.text: The Ijaw kingdom of Nembe, 30 miles up the Brass river, was poorer than Bonny and Calabar until the British blockade of those ports in the 19th century sent the slave ships to its creeks. Its line goes back to King Ogio, around 1639. A civil war split the city early in the 19th century into Ogbolomabiri and Bassambiri; trade moved to Twon-Brass on the coast as palm oil replaced slaves. In January 1895 King William Koko led over a thousand warriors against the Royal Niger Company's headquarters at Akassa, and the British sacked Nembe in reprisal amid a smallpox epidemic.

snapshots.title: Nembe in the creeks
snapshots.text: Nembe grows as an Ijaw kingdom; tradition dates its tenth king, Ogio, to around 1639.

snapshots.title: King Ogio's line
snapshots.text: Tradition names Ogio, the tenth king, around 1639, as the ancestor of all later kings. Nembe becomes a trading state once Europeans reach the coast, but stays poorer than Bonny and Calabar.

snapshots.title: Two towns, and the slave ships come
snapshots.text: A civil war splits Nembe: early in the 19th century King Ogbodo and his followers move to a new town at Bassambiri, while King Mingi stays at Nembe city (Ogbolomabiri). From the 1820s, as the British navy blockades Bonny and Calabar, slavers turn to the Brass river, and Nembe's position 30 miles upstream becomes an advantage.

snapshots.title: Two towns and a port
snapshots.text: By 1856 palm oil has overtaken slaves and the trade moves down to Twon-Brass on the coast. In 1863 Nembe decisively beats Kalabari, and it sometimes sides with Bonny against Kalabari. Ogbolomabiri takes a Christian mission in 1867 while Bassambiri does not, deepening the split.

snapshots.title: The Akassa raid
snapshots.text: After 1884 Britain claims Nembe within the Oil Rivers Protectorate. Nembe, which now controls the palm-oil trade, refuses a treaty and resists the Royal Niger Company's monopoly. In January 1895 King William Koko leads more than a thousand warriors in a dawn attack on the Company's headquarters at Akassa. Sir Frederick Bedford's force captures and sacks Nembe in reprisal, while smallpox ravages the kingdom. The British rule from a consulate at Twon-Brass.

today.text: Nembe has several Amanyanabos, for Ogbolomabiri, Bassambiri, Okpoama, Odioama and Twon-Brass, in Bayelsa State.
